subtitle: Optional background on regional culture frameworks: where they come from, what they measured, and why clusters say nothing about any person or about Minnesota communities.
audience: Optional, for DHS and DSD employees who have met a regional chart or cultural profile at work, or who are curious where those charts come from. No other course depends on it.

lessons.title: What regional frameworks are, and what they say nothing about
objectives: Describe how the GLOBE research program grouped societies into ten cultural clusters.
Name the ten GLOBE societal clusters.
Explain what the cluster data measured and what it did not measure.
Explain why clusters say nothing about any person or about Minnesota communities.
lessons.teaching:
You may come across charts that sort the world into regions and describe how people in each supposedly communicate or lead. Most of them draw on cluster frameworks, and the best known of these comes from the GLOBE research program, a large international study of culture and leadership. GLOBE researchers surveyed roughly seventeen thousand managers in about sixty societies about the practices and values they saw in their organizations and societies. They then grouped societies whose responses were similar. A study by Vipin Gupta, Paul Hanges and Peter Dorfman tested proposed groupings statistically and found support for ten clusters: Anglo, Germanic Europe, Nordic Europe, Latin Europe, Eastern Europe, Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, Arab (named Middle East in some later GLOBE writing), South Asia and Confucian Asia.

Clusters are useful because they give a big-picture map. They suggest where societies tended to be similar in, for example, how much they emphasized hierarchy, group loyalty or planning for the future, and where they tended to differ. For someone new to intercultural work, a map like this can make visible that one's own workplace habits are part of a pattern too, and it can suggest questions to ask before a meeting with a new partner. David Livermore’s short book Expand Your Borders (2013) is one overview written for this purpose. The list above is GLOBE’s. Livermore’s Leading with Cultural Intelligence (3rd ed., 2024, appendix, about pp. 233-39) names ten clusters of his own: Anglo, Arab, Confucian Asia, Eastern Europe, Germanic Europe, Latin America, Latin Europe, Nordic Europe, Southern Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. The names follow GLOBE’s, and his says Southern Asia where GLOBE says South Asia. His appendix cites Ronen and Shenkar (1985), and he gives no published source for where each cluster sits on his ten dimensions, so do not read his placements as GLOBE’s or as tested. He says himself that clusters are only one way to begin, that there is enormous variety inside each, and that many groups, including Indigenous populations, African Americans and Caribbean groups, have little affinity with any of them (about p. 233). These applications do not reproduce his profiles, country lists, placements or tables. The program’s practice courses used to be organized by region. They now start from work situations, and this optional course is where the regional framework lives.

It is just as important to know what the data did not measure. The respondents were managers in organizations, not a cross-section of each society. The results are averages for societies, usually countries, not descriptions of individuals. They were collected at a particular time, and societies change. Many people and peoples do not fit national boundaries: the Hmong live across several countries, Dakota and Anishinaabe nations are sovereign nations within what is now Minnesota, and many Minnesotans have heritage in more than one society or grew up here with parents from elsewhere. Religious, linguistic, regional and class differences within a country do not show up in a national average. Introductory textbooks that teach GLOBE make the same point, warning that relying solely on such frameworks can be misleading.

So hold two ideas together. Cluster research is real, careful work that can help you notice patterns, including your own. And a cluster describes a statistical tendency across a group of societies. Clusters say nothing about any person, and they say nothing about Minnesota communities. They were not built from Minnesota residents, and they cannot tell you how the person on the other side of the table communicates, decides or builds trust. To learn about a community here, go to the program’s community briefs and to the people themselves. The rest of this course is about using the map without mistaking it for the territory.
lessons.keyPoint: GLOBE’s ten clusters group societies by similarities in managers’ survey responses. They say nothing about any person or about Minnesota communities.
lessons.example: Practice case: Before a video call with a provider association whose leaders include several people who emigrated from Latin America, Grace, a DSD contract manager, skims a summary of the Latin America cluster. It notes a tendency, on average, to place value on relationships and group loyalty. Grace plans to open the call with ten minutes of personal conversation and to avoid discussing the contract details until the end. Her colleague Luis, who grew up in Minneapolis, says the association's leaders are known for being very businesslike.
lessons.question: What is the best way for Grace to use what she read?
choices: Keep her plan, since the cluster research is based on thousands of respondents.
Ignore the cluster summary entirely, since Luis has more direct knowledge.

Treat the summary as no evidence about these leaders and only as a reminder to prepare for more than one style: set a clear agenda with room for relationship building, and ask them at the start how they would like to use the time.
feedback: The size of the study makes the averages reliable for societies. It does not make the summary evidence about these leaders, who are business leaders working in Minnesota. The summary's only use is as a reminder to prepare for more than one style and to ask them.

Luis's knowledge is valuable, but it is secondhand, and the mistake is using it as a verdict. The summary is not evidence about these leaders either. Its only use is as a reminder to prepare for more than one style and to ask them.

This is the strongest response. The summary is not evidence about these leaders. Grace uses it only as a reminder to prepare for more than one style and to ask them, so the people involved shape the meeting.
lessons.reflection: When you read about a cultural pattern tied to a region, what is your first instinct: to apply it, to reject it, or to test it? What shapes that instinct?
lessons.action: Find a regional chart or cultural profile you have seen at work. Write down one pattern it describes and two reasons a specific person with heritage in that region might not fit it.

check.question: What did the GLOBE cluster research primarily measure?
check.correct: Average responses from managers in organizations about practices and values in their societies, grouped into clusters of similar societies.
wrong: The personality traits of every person living in each country.
Which cultures are more effective or advanced than others.
check.feedback: GLOBE compared societies using managers' survey responses. It produced averages for societies, not profiles of individuals, and grouping societies by similarity is not the same as ranking them.

lessons.title: Cultural intelligence: drive, knowledge, strategy and action
objectives: Define cultural intelligence as the capability to relate and work effectively in culturally diverse situations.
Distinguish the four capabilities: drive, knowledge, strategy and action.
Explain why cluster knowledge is only one of the four capabilities.
Identify one way to build each capability in DHS or DSD work.
lessons.teaching:
Cultural intelligence, often called CQ®, is defined by the Cultural Intelligence Center as the capability to function effectively in culturally diverse situations. David Livermore’s Leading with Cultural Intelligence (3rd ed., 2024), which anchors these applications, uses Soon Ang and Linn Van Dyne’s definition: the capability “to relate and work effectively in culturally diverse situations” (chapter 1, about p. 3). He extends it past nationality to what he calls figured worlds, the settings where we work out who we are. The idea grew out of academic research, including work by Soon Ang, Linn Van Dyne and colleagues, who developed a twenty-item scale and tested it across samples in the United States and Singapore. Their studies found that different parts of cultural intelligence were related to different outcomes, such as the quality of cultural judgments and decisions, adjustment in new cultural settings, and task performance in culturally diverse work. The research describes four related capabilities, which the Cultural Intelligence Center names drive, knowledge, strategy and action.

Drive is motivation: interest in and confidence about working across cultures, and willingness to persist when it is uncomfortable. Knowledge is understanding how cultures are similar and different, including frameworks like the GLOBE clusters, knowledge of languages, faith practices and history, and awareness of your own cultural patterns. Strategy is using that knowledge to plan and to make sense of what is happening: preparing for an interaction, noticing when something is not working, and checking assumptions as you go. Action is behaving flexibly and appropriately, such as adjusting how directly you speak, how you use silence, or how you open a meeting. Livermore gives each capability parts: intrinsic interest, extrinsic interest and self-efficacy for drive; cultural-general and context-specific for knowledge; planning, awareness and checking for strategy; and speech acts, verbal and nonverbal for action (chapter 2, about pp. 27-33).

Notice where cluster frameworks sit. They feed knowledge, one capability out of four. Knowledge without strategy can become stereotyping, because nothing prompts you to check whether a pattern applies, a risk Livermore names himself (chapter 5, about pp. 123-24). Knowledge without drive can stay on the shelf. Knowledge without action changes nothing about how the meeting goes. This is why the program’s practice courses start from work situations and questions, not from descriptions of regions. The program’s Cultural Intelligence collection is also broader than these four capabilities.

The Cultural Intelligence Center describes these capabilities as skills that can be developed through education, training and experience, depending on how people reflect on those experiences. That fits public service well. A case manager preparing for a first visit, a supervisor planning a meeting with a new team, and a policy analyst designing a listening session with county and Tribal partners can each work on all four capabilities. Most of this research is self-reported and gathered at one point in time, so it shows association rather than cause, and researchers still debate how distinct cultural intelligence is from related abilities such as emotional intelligence. We found no studies specific to disability services or a state human-services workforce, so applying these ideas here is the program’s own judgment. Some organizations use commercial assessments of cultural intelligence. This course does not assess anyone, and nothing here should be used to rate colleagues. CQ® is a registered trademark of Cultural Intelligence Center, LLC. These applications are not affiliated with Cultural Intelligence Center, LLC, or with David Livermore. They do not use the licensed CQ scale or show CQ scores.
lessons.keyPoint: Cultural intelligence has four capabilities: drive, knowledge, strategy and action. Cluster frameworks feed knowledge only; strategy is what turns knowledge into questions instead of stereotypes.
lessons.example: Practice case: Jin, a new DSD supervisor, has read several regional culture summaries and can describe patterns for most of the ten clusters. In team meetings, though, she runs the agenda the same way every time and is surprised when some staff rarely speak. Her manager, Paula, suggests she look at how she is using what she knows. Paula points out that two quieter staff members wrote thoughtful comments on a draft afterward, so they clearly have views to share.
lessons.question: Which capability would most help Jin right now?
choices: Strategy: planning how to check what helps each person contribute, and noticing during meetings when her approach is not working.
More knowledge: reading the remaining cluster summaries in more detail.
Drive: telling herself to be more enthusiastic about diversity.
feedback: This is the strongest response. Jin already has knowledge. What is missing is using it to plan, observe and adjust, and to ask people rather than predict them.
More reading adds knowledge without addressing the gap, and could increase the risk of assuming patterns about staff.
Jin's interest seems genuine already. Enthusiasm alone will not change how her meetings run.
lessons.reflection: Of the four capabilities, which feels strongest for you and which gets the least attention? What is one small situation this month where you could practice the weaker one?
lessons.action: Before your next meeting that includes people with different working styles, write down one assumption you hold about how the meeting should run and one way you will check it during the meeting.

check.question: Where do cluster frameworks like GLOBE fit among the four capabilities of cultural intelligence?
check.correct: They contribute to knowledge, one of four capabilities, and need strategy to be checked against real people and situations.
wrong: They are the whole of cultural intelligence.
They belong to action, because knowing a cluster tells you exactly how to behave.
check.feedback: Frameworks are knowledge. Cultural intelligence also needs motivation, planning and checking, and flexible behavior. Treating a framework as a behavior script skips the strategy step, which is where assumptions get tested.

lessons.title: The ecological fallacy: group averages do not predict individuals
objectives: Define the ecological fallacy in plain language.
Explain why a society-level average cannot tell you where any individual falls.
Identify examples of the ecological fallacy in everyday workplace and service decisions.
Compare a stereotype with a pattern used only to write a question.
lessons.teaching:
The ecological fallacy is the error of assuming that relationships observed for groups necessarily hold for individuals. The statistician David Freedman explained it with a classic example: finding higher suicide rates in societies with more Protestants does not show that Protestants themselves were more likely to die by suicide. Group data and individual data answer different questions. A pattern across groups can even reverse when you look at individuals.

Cluster frameworks are group data. If the average response from one cluster's managers leaned toward respect for hierarchy, that tells you something about the societies in that cluster compared with others. It does not tell you whether a particular colleague who grew up in one of those societies prefers a hierarchical style. The spread of individuals within a society is usually wide, and the averages of two societies can differ while many individuals from each overlap. Add migration, generation, profession, faith, disability, personal history and the organizational culture of DHS itself, and the distance between a society's average and one person's style grows further.

In practice, the ecological fallacy shows up in small moments. A hiring panelist reads a candidate's hesitation to self-promote as a cultural trait rather than asking a follow-up question. A supervisor assumes a new employee from a certain region will not want to disagree in meetings and stops inviting their view. A case manager assumes a family from a particular country will not want outside help. Each takes a real pattern and applies it to a person who never had a chance to show whether it fits. Stereotypes are often built this way: not from invented facts, but from true averages misapplied.

Livermore calls research-based tendencies sophisticated stereotypes and says to hold them loosely and learn from direct contact what the person wants (chapter 1, about pp. 21-22). He still keeps them as a starting point about a person. These applications go further. A pattern can produce a question to ask or a change to make in a system. It never produces an expectation of the person, and asking the person remains the rule. When you need something before you meet someone, do not guess: offer options, and let the person choose. When answers may be shaped by who holds power, change how and by whom you ask, and never conclude that the person cannot say. A useful test: would I be comfortable if this person knew I was making this assumption about them, and could I explain how I would find out if I was wrong? If the answer is no, you are probably predicting rather than preparing. Decisions that carry real consequences, such as hiring, discipline, eligibility or service planning, must rest on the individual facts and the responsible process, not on a pattern about the person's presumed group.
lessons.keyPoint: A cluster average describes a group of societies, not the person in front of you. Turn a pattern into a question, not an expectation, and let people tell you; never base consequential decisions on group averages.
lessons.example: Practice case: On a hiring panel for a DSD policy role, Mark notes that one candidate, Wei, gave short answers about her own accomplishments and often said "we" instead of "I." Mark says this is typical of the Confucian Asia cluster and suggests the panel mentally adjust her scores upward. Another panelist, Ingrid, is uneasy but is not sure why. The panel's scoring guide asks every candidate to describe a policy project they led and their specific role in it.
lessons.question: What should Ingrid say?
choices: Agree with Mark, since adjusting for cultural style is a fair thing to do.

Point out that Wei's answers should be scored against the job-related criteria like everyone's, and suggest the panel use a consistent follow-up prompt, such as asking every candidate what their own role was, raising any scoring questions with Human Resources.
Say that culture has nothing to do with interview behavior, so the panel should score the answers as given with no follow-up.
feedback: Mark's intent is generous, but guessing Wei's style from a cluster average and adjusting her score is the ecological fallacy and is not a consistent, job-related process.

This is the strongest response. It avoids assumptions about Wei's background, gives every candidate the same chance to explain their contribution, and keeps scoring questions with the responsible office.
Styles of talking about accomplishments can differ for many reasons, including culture. Refusing any structured follow-up leaves a possible barrier in place for all candidates.
lessons.reflection: Can you recall a time someone assumed something about you based on a group you belong to, even a flattering assumption? What would you have preferred they do?
lessons.action: Before your next interview panel, planning meeting or first visit, write down one assumption you notice yourself making about a person based on a group. Then write the question you will ask, of everyone, to find out instead.

check.question: Which statement is an example of the ecological fallacy?
check.correct: Because one cluster's average leaned toward indirect communication, this colleague from that region must prefer indirect feedback.
wrong: Averages for two clusters differed on how they rated hierarchy.
Individuals within the same society vary widely in communication style.
check.feedback: Comparing group averages is a legitimate use of group data, and recognizing individual variation is accurate. The fallacy is moving from a group average to a conclusion about a particular person.

lessons.title: Turning a cluster pattern into questions in everyday work
objectives: Plan how to turn a cluster pattern into a question.
Distinguish preparing for more than one style from predicting a single style.
Explain how to drop a pattern based on what a person or partner tells you.
Draft a short preparation note for a meeting using this question-first approach.
lessons.teaching:
If you do use a cluster pattern, and you never have to, how should you use it? The answer is to turn it into a question you ask, never an expectation of the person. This is the planning, awareness and checking part of cultural intelligence. It uses knowledge to widen what you prepare for, rather than narrow what you expect.

A simple sequence works well. First, name the pattern: "Research suggests societies in this cluster tended, on average, to place more emphasis on relationships before business." Second, turn it on yourself: what is my own default here, and what would I miss if the meeting ran only that way? If you are used to getting straight to the agenda, that is also a cultural pattern, and it may be the one that needs adjusting. Third, list the options you can offer: a clear agenda, time for introductions for those who want it, and more than one way to contribute. Fourth, ask, and let the person choose: "How would you like to use our time today?" Fifth, revise: what the person tells you replaces the pattern. Then, importantly, do not carry that person's preference onto the next person from the same region.

One further habit keeps those questions honest: look beyond national culture. DHS has its own organizational culture, professions have norms, disability communities have cultures, and generations differ. A county social worker and a state policy analyst from the same background may still work very differently.

Livermore also names ten dimensions (chapter 5, about pp. 98-124): individualism versus collectivism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance, cooperative versus competitive, short term versus long term, context as direct versus indirect, being versus doing, universalism versus particularism, neutral versus affective, and monochronic versus polychronic. These applications use them only to notice your own defaults, to discuss your team’s norms and to ask what a process assumes, never to place a group or to predict a person. The CQ Knowledge course turns each one into a question to ask yourself.

In DHS and DSD work, this approach has a narrow use: noticing your own defaults and widening what you prepare for. It tells you nothing about a Minnesota community or the person you are meeting. To learn about them, go to the program's community briefs, community partners and the people served. It never justifies treating someone differently in a formal decision. A framework can remind you to prepare for more than one style. The people you work with give you the answers.
lessons.keyPoint: Use a cluster pattern only to name your own default and widen the options you prepare. Then ask, let the person choose, and revise. Never carry one person's answer onto the next person.
lessons.example: Practice case: Fatima, a DSD program specialist, is preparing for her first meeting with a new Tribal liaison, Joseph, and a county supervisor, Linda, to plan a joint training. Fatima wants to use what she has read in some regional culture summaries. She has also read that tribal governments have their own protocols. She is unsure how to prepare without making assumptions about either person.
lessons.question: What preparation approach is best?
choices: Prepare a clear draft agenda with space for introductions, ask both at the start how they would like to proceed, and check with DHS Tribal relations staff about any protocol that applies to working with the Tribal government.
Use the Anglo cluster profile for Linda and skip preparation for Joseph, since Tribal nations are not in the cluster data.
Avoid preparing at all, so she does not bring any assumptions into the room.
feedback: This is the strongest response. Fatima prepares for a range of styles, lets both people shape the meeting, and recognizes that working with a sovereign nation's representative involves protocols she should learn from the right office rather than from cluster research.

Assigning Linda a cluster profile from a guess about her background is the ecological fallacy, and noticing that the cluster data does not cover Tribal nations should lead to asking, not to less preparation.
Skipping preparation does not remove assumptions; it just leaves your own defaults unexamined.
lessons.reflection: Think about an upcoming interaction with someone whose working style you do not yet know. What is your own default style, and how might it shape the meeting if you do not name it?
lessons.action: Write a short preparation note for one upcoming meeting: your own default, one or two other styles to prepare for, the question you will ask to find out, and how you will adjust.

check.question: What is the main difference between using a cluster pattern as a source of questions and using it as a stereotype?
check.correct: A question leaves the answer to the person and is asked fresh of each person; a stereotype is applied as a fixed expectation.
wrong: A question is based on research, while a stereotype is always invented.
Questions are only used by researchers, not in daily work.
check.feedback: Stereotypes are often built on real patterns, so the difference is not where the idea came from. It is what you do with it: whether the person has room to show you who they are, and whether you revise and move on.

cards.back: Ten groups of societies with similar average survey responses about cultural practices and values: Anglo, Germanic Europe, Nordic Europe, Latin Europe, Eastern Europe, Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, Arab or Middle East, South Asia and Confucian Asia. They say nothing about any person or about Minnesota communities.
The capability to function effectively in culturally diverse situations, described as four capabilities: drive, knowledge, strategy and action.
The error of assuming that relationships observed for groups necessarily hold for individuals.
A pattern used only to widen what you prepare for and to write a question you would ask anyone. It never sets an expectation of the person.
Using knowledge to plan for an interaction, notice when something is not working, and check assumptions as you go.

aid.heading: Before you use a cluster profile
items: Remember it describes averages for societies, based mostly on managers' responses.
Name your own default style first.
List reasons a specific person might not fit, such as migration, generation, faith, profession or disability.
Check whether the person's people or nation is covered at all; Tribal nations and peoples who live across borders are not.

aid.heading: Turn a pattern into a question
items: State the pattern as a tendency of societies, not a fact about a person.
List the options you can offer.
Ask, using questions you would ask anyone, and let the person choose.
Revise, and do not carry one person's answer onto the next.

aid.heading: Guardrails
items: Never use a cluster to describe a Minnesota community or any person.
Never use a cluster profile in hiring, discipline, eligibility or service decisions.
Do not rate or label colleagues' cultural intelligence.
Use community briefs, partners and the people served as your main sources.
Use Tribal relations staff and consultation processes for work with Tribal nations.

Paraphrased; its tables, placements and cluster profiles are not reproduced. Where these applications differ, the course says so. Livermore is a founder of the Cultural Intelligence Center. Applications to disability and public service are not his.
